articles.title: SJAA EPHEMERIS
articles.summary: The SJAA Ephemeris is the official publication of the San Jose Astronomical Association, specifically for September 1995. It is identified as Volume 6, Number 9, indicating a regular newsletter or magazine from the organization.

articles.title: The Eyepiece
articles.summary: This column reports on a recent less-than-excellent viewing experience at Fremont Peak, highlighting a persistent insect problem and offering practical solutions. It also provides updates on early Ephemeris publication and upcoming USPS rule changes for non-profits. A detailed calendar for September and October outlines numerous astronomical events, including star parties, general meetings, an observational astronomy class, and a 40th-year anniversary dinner for the San Jose Astronomical Association.

articles.title: Forty Years Ago this month
articles.summary: This article recounts a September meeting of an astronomy club, led by President Walt Krumm, featuring presentations on a recent convention, the constellations Pegasus and Andromeda, and detailed instructions on making telescope tripods. Following the meeting, members gathered for an hour of observing in Columbus Park. The piece also briefly touches on club activities, an internal policy debate, and lists the club's officers.

articles.title: MOONWATCH
articles.summary: Don Watson recounts his experiences with the "Moonwatch" program in the late 1950s/early 1960s, where amateur astronomers, including his Cincinnati Astronomical Society team, were tasked with tracking early artificial satellites after the launch of the first Russian satellite. His team leveraged early IBM mainframe computers and a Fortran program developed by student Tom van Flandern to generate satellite predictions, aiding their observations and fostering friendly competition with other groups. Watson shares personal anecdotes about the challenges and rewards of this pioneering effort in citizen science.

articles.title: Henry Coe State Park
articles.summary: A star party held at Henry Coe State Park on July 22 was successful despite challenging high winds that made high-power viewing difficult. Attendees observed various deep-sky objects like M4, M22, M24, and M11, along with Jupiter and Saturn. The highlight was the successful search, finding, and verification of the motion of Comet 6P/d'Arrest.

articles.title: Astronomical Humour
articles.summary: This article features a humorous anecdote from Isaac Asimov, where he recounts his extensive experience explaining complex scientific concepts like wave-particle duality. He humorously notes that he's become so adept that at dinner parties, guests conspire to avoid asking him about it, leaving him "primed and aching to explain" but never given the opportunity.

articles.title: Heartbreak of Optics
articles.summary: Bill Marriott recounts a 'heartbreak' incident where he accidentally cracked a large Bk-7 glass slab due to thermal shock, despite his own cautions about the material's sensitivity. Drawing inspiration from a historical account of a cracked 60-inch mirror blank, he quickly sourced alternative glass plates from a supplier. He is now considering how to utilize these new blanks for various optical projects, such as an optical window or a Schmidt corrector, while continuing his other ongoing work.

articles.title: METEOR SCATTER - the FAQs
articles.summary: This FAQ document, revised July 1995, provides basic information about meteor scatter (MS) for amateur astronomers, radio amateurs, and schools. It explains MS as the temporary reflection of radio waves by ionized meteor trails (100-80 km altitude) and clarifies that meteors do not generate radio emissions themselves. The guide outlines how to observe MS by tuning to empty VHF frequencies to pick up distant broadcast stations, highlighting its utility for studying daylight meteor streams and secure communication.

articles.title: Meteors - continued from page three
articles.summary: This article serves as a guide for radio meteor observation, detailing suitable frequencies (40-144 MHz) and recommended equipment such as FM receivers and Yagi antennas. It explains how to identify and record meteor reflections, discusses potential interferences like sporadic-E, and offers insights into relating radio observations to visual ones. The text also covers methods for correcting observed meteor counts and lists resources for meteor stream data.

articles.title: Meteors
articles.summary: This document provides resources for meteor observation, particularly focusing on radio meteor science. It directs readers to online sources for meteor stream overviews, observational data, and reduction software, as well as the monthly RMOB for global observation summaries. Key references include foundational books like 'Meteor Science and Engineering' and 'Meteor Burst Communications,' along with relevant astronomy periodicals.

articles.title: Periodical Publication Statement
articles.summary: The SJAA Ephemeris, the monthly newsletter of the San Jose Astronomical Association, is published 12 times a year from January to December. It is provided as a service included with membership and is also distributed to other astronomy clubs, publishers, and selected individuals.

articles.title: My new 1.16" f/34 Schiefspiegler
articles.summary: Frustrated by poor views of Jupiter through his Meade 2045D SC in humid Texas skies, Bob Rogers improvised a '1.16" f/34 Schiefspiegler' by adding a card stock disk with a small hole to his telescope. This simple modification significantly improved image contrast, allowing him to discern both the Northern and Southern dark zones on Jupiter, which were previously hard to see. The document also includes an astronomy club calendar for late 1995.

articles.title: Telescope Loaner Status
articles.summary: This document provides a status update for a telescope loaner program, detailing various telescopes, their current users, and due dates. It indicates which telescopes are currently available for loan, specifies conditions for borrowing a solar telescope, and includes a waitlist and instructions for members to request an instrument.

articles.title: ASTRO ADS
articles.summary: The "ASTRO ADS" section provides free classifieds for noncommercial advertisers to sell astronomically related products or services. This particular section includes a 'lost' ad for an SJAA battery left at Fremont Peak, as well as two 'for sale' ads for a 12-1/2 inch f/9 Ritchy Chretien telescope and an 8-inch f/8 Newtonian telescope.

articles.title: Notice
articles.summary: The article announces that John Dobson will be celebrating his 80th birthday in September. A Star Party is scheduled for September 1st at Houge Park to honor him for his significant contributions to amateur astronomy and astronomy education.

articles.title: Lunar Phase Date Rise Trans Set
articles.summary: This document provides a tabular overview of key lunar phases, including First Quarter, Full Moon, Last Quarter, and New Moon. For each phase, it lists the corresponding date and the moon's rise, transit, and set times, offering a concise astronomical reference.

articles.title: Nearer Planets
articles.summary: This document provides an astronomical guide for observing the 'nearer planets' including Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn. For three specific dates (the 7th, 17th, and 27th), it lists each planet's approximate distance from the sun in Astronomical Units (A.U.), apparent magnitude, and three associated observing times.

articles.title: SOL Star Type G2V
articles.summary: This document identifies the subject as "SOL Star Type G2V," referring to our Sun. It presents a concise tabular dataset that appears to list celestial coordinates (Right Ascension and Declination) along with additional numerical values across several entries, possibly for tracking or reference.

articles.title: Astronomical Twilight
articles.summary: The document presents a table detailing the start and end times for astronomical twilight across several Julian Dates. This data illustrates the shifting duration and timing of astronomical twilight over a period of approximately one month.

articles.title: Sidereal Time
articles.summary: This document provides sidereal time transit data, specifically Right Ascension at Local Midnight, for various dates in September. It also details specific astronomical event times—sunset, twilight end, moonset, and dawn begin—for 'Darkest Saturday Night' on September 23, 1995.

articles.title: Officers and Board of Directors
articles.summary: This document lists the current officers and board of directors, including their names, titles (President, Vice President, Treasurer, Secretary, and Directors), and respective contact phone numbers. It serves as a directory for the organization's leadership.

articles.title: Ephemeris Contributors
articles.summary: The article 'Ephemeris Contributors' provides a list of individuals who contribute to ephemeris data. It includes their names and associated phone numbers, serving as a contact directory for these contributors.

articles.title: COMET COMMENTS
articles.summary: The article provides updates on several comets, noting that Periodic Comet d'Arrest is dimming while Periodic Comet Jackson-Neujmin is slightly brightening. The primary focus is the independent discovery of Comet 1995 O1 (Hale-Bopp) by Alan Hale and Thomas Bopp on July 23, 1995, detailing their discovery circumstances and early indications that the comet is distant and will be visible for an extended period.

articles.title: EPHEMERIS
articles.summary: This document provides ephemeris data for several comets, including 96P/d'ARREST and 1994 d1 (HALE-BOPP), detailing their celestial coordinates (Right Ascension, Declination), elongation, and predicted sky magnitudes for observation periods in late 1995. It also lists orbital elements like perihelion date and distance for these comets. The information, compiled by Don Machholz, serves as an observing guide, noting that orbital data for P/JACKSON-NEUJMIN 1995O is approximate due to insufficient precision.

articles.title: SAN JOSE ASTRONOMICAL ASSOCIATION MEMBERSHIP
articles.summary: The San Jose Astronomical Association (SJAA) publishes a monthly newsletter called "EPHEMERIS" and encourages members to submit articles for publication. Submissions should be typed and sent to the editor, Bob Madden, by the 12th of the previous month, preferably as a text file on a 3-1/2" IBM or MAC diskette, but written submissions are also accepted.

articles.title: SAN JOSE ASTRONOMICAL ASSOCIATION MEMBERSHIP
articles.summary: This document is a membership application form for the San Jose Astronomical Association (SJAA). It details various membership types and their associated fees, including options for individual, S&T magazine inclusive, and junior memberships. The form provides instructions for submission to the treasurer and payment details, along with the organization's mailing address.

articles.title: SJAA HOTLINE
articles.summary: The document, titled "SJAA HOTLINE," provides a 24-hour information phone number (408-559-1221) for the SJAA. It references an ephemeris from September 1995, suggesting it's a resource for astronomical data and club-related information.
